writing.explanation:
For [3,1,5,2], initialize the carried maximum to the smallest representable value. Reading rightward state in reverse yields 2,5,5,5; writing each at its original index produces [5,5,5,2].

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return the suffix maximum at every index. The visible fixture is `[3, 1, 5, 2]` and its example result is `5,5,5,2`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Suffix Aggregate when it asks for right-side maxima, suffix totals, partition checks. Here the concrete task is: Return the suffix maximum at every index. The visible input `[3, 1, 5, 2]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Precomputation pays when many ranges are queried. If values change between queries, an updateable structure may be needed; for one small query, a direct walk is simpler. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Precompute information from right to left for queries about everything after a position. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? A range method summarizes intervals so the same information is not recomputed. A static prefix table and an updateable tree make different tradeoffs; define endpoint conventions first. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n) build · O(1) query · O(n) space; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `5,5,5,2` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test the first and last position, an empty range where permitted, and the boundary immediately after an update. Allocate an extra prefix slot when a zero-length prefix simplifies indexing, and use a numeric type large enough for accumulated values. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
